title: R.U.R.
subtitle: Rossum's Universal Robots
publisher: English version by Paul Selver and Nigel Playfair, Doubleday, Page (1923)
pitch: The 1920 play that gave the world the word robot. A factory makes artificial workers, the world comes to depend on them, and the robots rise up.

chapters.g: Helena Glory visits the island factory of Rossum's Universal Robots, where artificial people are made to work, and stays.
Ten years later, robots have spread everywhere, humans have stopped having children, and a robot revolt begins.
The last humans are besieged in the factory and try to bargain for their lives.
Alquist, the last man, watches two robots discover something new.

ideas: Robot comes from the Czech word for forced labour.
Making minds to serve us may backfire.
Dependence on artificial workers can hollow out society.
The new beings may inherit what is human.

args.a: The play warns that creating servant minds leads to revolt.
args.c: Capek's robots are closer to artificial humans than to machines, and the play is also about factory work and capitalism.

args.a: Humans lose purpose when machines do all the work.
args.c: Others argue freedom from toil could let people flourish.

questions: Is it wrong to build a mind to be a servant?
What does the ending suggest about the future?

quiz.q: What word did this play give the world?
What do humans stop doing in Act Two?
quiz.w: A sign of society hollowing out.
